The men of the services require rehabilitation, and our civilian industries require reconversion. The men of the services will receive pensions and gratuities; our civilian groups would like to be able to enjoy lighter taxes. Both groups are concerned with homes and jobs. Previous speakers on this motion have dealt adequately with the subject, so that I shall leave it now and pass on to what I think the service men would like to be reassured about with regard to the attitude of this house and the present parliament.
I think they would ask first of us that we produce as much of a feeling of national unity as is possible in any community. I know they would ask of us a fearless approach to our national problems. In the past they have been controversial and they must be solved to help Canada's progress. I know the services would say to the government to-day, bring them down, bring them before every party and group in this house; let them see the light of day and let us face them fearlessly.
Many men and women in the services have obtained a wide knowledge of Canada during their time in the war. They have seen many provinces; overseas they have fought beside Canadians of all races and creeds from all parts of the dominion. They cannot tolerate any longer the petty divisions which seem up to this time to have been so easy of exploitation by politicians in this country. I know they would have us make an end of all these that can possibly be buried. If they have been as fortunate as I have they would have seen all the provinces with the exception of Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia. They

The Address-Mr. Skey
would have enjoyed the friendliness of Prince Edward Island, seen its red soil and its potato fields and tasted its lobsters and oysters. They would have met the friendly people of Nova Scotia and formed an idea of the great contribution of that province to the building of our mighty Canadian navy. They would have seen the woods and farms of New Brunswick, and maybe they would have had the experience, which I had some months ago, of flying over that province and witnessing from the air a forest fire which was consuming the wealth of the province and apparently ranging unchecked. They would have seen the historic capital of the province of Quebec and cosmopolitan Montreal. I happen to have lived in Ontario; I was born there and have travelled over it widely; and for three years I was resident in friendly Manitoba. The rest of the provinces of Canada it is my intention to see before the close of this parliament, and I hope that other hon. members among us will travel as the hon. member for Davenport (iMr. MacNicol) has done and investigate all the provinces and become acquainted with the people of all provinces and tongues and faiths in our dominion.
Before I speak about my own service, the air force, I should like to pay humble tribute as an air force officer to our Canadian army and navy. The army, fighting for the first time as an integral unit, suffered a long, hard struggle in Italy, then gallantly marched into Normandy, and from there through the Netherlands, Belgium and Germany to the Baltic sea. They displayed in siege and battle the greatest powers of invention and endurance.
In my experience in the air force I have had a lot to do with the Canadian navy and with the 'Royal Navy. I have witnessed their phenomenal growth, their vigilance in the home waters and on the broad Atlantic, and seen the way in which they have admirably discharged their tremendous responsibilities of convoy escort.
Turning for a moment to our branch of the service, I should like to give this house a short description of it. It is young; it is lusty; it is imaginative and it is still growing. Its members have fought alongside the army and navy of Canada and of other countries, and I know those other services will appreciate a claim that can be made for the air force, that they should have a certain amount of freedom to digest their immense expansion and the immense power they achieved during war time.
I would commend to this house the stand that has already been taken by the government in allowing the ministry for air to remain separate for some time. It may take the air force as long as from two to three years to
get straightened away on its new path in peace, and I would commend leaving it to its own growth until it has achieved full manhood and adjusted the new factors which have so recently brought it into discussion again. The air force at present requires a policy for peace. Young men, good men, able men, technicians, pilots and men whose knowledge and duties cover all the services that it governs would like to stay with it. It has seized their imagination, and they would like to stay with it and play a part in the future defence of Canada, should that ever be necessary. They would like to know what the government has to offer them in the way of a career.
I should like now to pass on for a moment and speak on the subject of technical research.
I am sure that when the appreciation of this war is written historians will give to the technical capacity of the scientists of the united nations, England, the United States and our own great Canada, credit for a tremendous achievement, that they will judge that our scientific potential was, apart from the will of our people to fight, the dominant factor in our victory.
I feel that our scientific potential is the greatest factor in our peace-time recovery and in our continued prosperity. Were I not such a junior member of this house I might go so far as to recommend that we have a ministry of technical research to which the heads of all services could take their problems,. to which industry, agriculture, medicine and all our other professions in Canada could go with their problems for solution and help.
In summing up my remarks, I should like to leave with the house the thought that the services and civilians alike would ask of this government, and ask of us, unity in Canada. I would put forward the suggestion that perhaps our wartime information board and the national film board, controlled by a joint parliamentary committee, could be used as two great instruments to teach all parts of Canada about their neighbours, their friends, about the problems of other provinces, and to educate us to a national outlook.
I believe that science and scientific research and technique as an aid to all Canadian businesses and to our services is the great need of the future. With no desire to delay the house any longer, may I say that in a few days' time hon. members will be asked to consider grants for the armed services. I have no information and no idea as to what these grants will be, but I would leave with the house this one thought. I believe it is necessary that we should keep the weapons of war in the hands of the people who love peace.
The Address-Mr. Dorion

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like first to join with the other speakers who have taken part in this debate in offering you my most sincere congratulations on the high honour conferred upon you unanimously by the House of Commons. In the last few years we have learned to know you, and I am sure that, with the sense of justice and equity which characterizes you, you will maintain the tradition that has been established by those who in the past have so illustriously occupied the seat which you hold at the present time. There is no doubt that this honour reflects also upon your family, and especially upon your country and also upon our province.
Since we last met in this chamber there have been many changes as a result of the general election of last June. Among the newcomers, particularly those from the province of Quebec, there are many young men who will n'o doubt be a valuable asset to the House of Commons. I would call attention to the fact that the bar of Quebec is very highly represented among the members. Some of them have already been called to fill important positions, as, for example, attorneys for the crown, members of the council of the bar, and a president of their association. Allow me to mention the present batonnier of the bar of Montreal, the hon. member for Stanstead (Mr. Hackett). I have no doubt that all these members will make their contribution to the keeping up of the good reputation of our bar, which has already furnished this house with a great many prominent members.
If on one side new representatives from the province of Quebec deserve the honour that has been conferred upon them by their electors, I cannot forget that unfortunately we have lost some members who for one reason or another were very close to some of the members of the house. I wish to mention my friend Mr. J. S. Roy, the previous member for Gaspe, who for the past five years sat in this house commanding the respect of all his fellow members. Even if we did not share his political views, I am sure that every member sitting in the last parliament had the utmost consideration for my former colleague, and I have no doubt it must have taken a capital man such as the present sitting member for Gaspe to defeat him.
As many hon. members have said in the course of this debate, and as we have also read in the newspapers throughout the country, the speech from the throne contains a few good suggestions. On the other hand, it is noticeable for its lack of measures which 
were expected by the people of the country. I note with satisfaction that the government has finally decided to bring before the house a policy providing for a national flag. I am sure that this decision will be welcomed by all fair-thinking citizens, by those who hold Canada above everything else, and by those who want to see our country secure its share of sovereignty. I am also pleased to note that the government has decided to define Canadian citizenship. I really believe that this is a new step toward what everybody wishes, and I sincerely hope that these two measures, when they come before the house for discussion, will be discussed with broadmindedness.
Mention was also made in the speech from the throne of the international part that our country is called upon to play, and I expect that when the appropriate measures dealing with this question are brought before the house we shall have an opportunity of expressing our point of view. I may state now that the events of the last years and particularly of the last months have changed to a certain extent the ideas one could have with regard to the important role that our country is called upon to play in international affairs.
(Translation): Mr. Speaker, if Canada is to play the part she is expected to take in the international sphere, and even if she is to weather the difficulties of the post-war period, she must, to my mind, fulfil two essential conditions. The first is that we should continue our march toward absolute independence; the second, that, we should find a fair and equitable solution to our domestic problems.
In order to fulfil the first condition, I think it would be necessary to destroy some remaining vestiges of the colonial spirit of old. The first and one of the most important of those vestiges is, I believe, the view that is taken in the matter of amendments to our constitution. As is well known, under the terms of the statute of Westminster, we are still compelled to go to the London parliament in order to obtain consent to any amendment to this country's constitution which we may want to bring about. That clause of the statute of Westminster, which was supposed to guarantee the rights of minorities in Canada, has indeed become a grave danger.
I could not illustrate that better than by mentioning what happened in 1943 on the occasion of the last amendment to our constitution. In July 1943, the House of Commons, following a discussion and by a majority vote, passed a resolution whereby an address was voted to His Majesty the King, requesting him to have the kindness to amend

The Address-Mr. Dorion
our constitution so that the redistribution, of electoral districts might be deferred, and on that occasion, when the resolution came up before the British House of Commons, it was thoroughly discussed. I have in hand the British House of Commons report of July 22, 1943-the date on which the Secretary of State for the Dominions, who then was Mr. Attlee the present Prime Minister, made his submission on the matter-and I shall quote the following excerpt from that statement:
At the time of the passing of the Statute of Westminster, an express provision was made at the request of the government of Canada, taking out from the general powers then conferred^ any power to amend or repeal the British North America Act. and the procedure therefore for amending the British North America Act remains as it was before the Statute of Westminster.
And in order to indicate what is meant by that clause of the statute of Westminster, I shall refer to a speech delivered by Mr. Edmund Harvey:
Mr. Edmund Harvey (Combined English universities): Surely the whole question depends on section 7 (1), of the act of Westminster, which was expressly put in at the request of Canada. I think that meets the point raised by the hon. gentleman the member for Altrincham (Sir E. Grigg). It was put in in order to protect the interests of certain minorities in Canada who at that period desired that, in the event of any change being requested by the Canadian parliament which they themselves did not unite in, there should remain the possibility of this parliament protecting the interests of the minority. It is an entirely exceptional position placed in the act.
I believe therefore, Mr. Speaker, that such are the exact wording and the true meaning of that clause inserted in the Statute of Westminster; for that reason, we must now wonder whether that clause, inserted for the protection of the rights of minorities, still constitutes the guarantee for which it was intended. In order to answer that question, I shall quote the speech delivered, in that same debate, by Sir Edward Grigg, and I quote:
Sir Edward Grigg (Altrincham):	I suggest
that it is really improper in present circumstances for the house to question the discretion of a sovereign parliament in the Commonwealth of Nations. It is only owing to a technical legislative peculiarity that it comes to the house at all, and it is very improper that the house should question the discretion of a national and absolutely sovereign parliament. I hope that that will be accepted by the house and that this legislation will be passed without further comment.
Which means, Mr. Speaker, that each time the Canadian parliament adopted a resolution similar to another brought down before the British House of Commons, the latter considered themselves bound by the majority vote given in this House of Commons and consequently cannot and will not discuss the
question as to whether or not such a procedure endangers the rights of minorities in this country. We must remember that on that occasion, one of the provinces had signified its unanimous opposition to this amendment to the Canadian constitution, therefore, it is obvious that the protection which existed in the past was no more existent. Therefore I think I am right in saying, as I said then in the debate in this house on the proposed amendment that our constitution has simply become an ordinary law which a majority can modify at will and according to the good pleasure of the party in power. That is why it is urgent that this government set up an organization to inquire anew into this matter of vital importance to us. I would suggest, for example, that the federal government set up a commission of jurists, appointed not only by the Canadian government but also by the governments of the different provinces of the dominion. However, great care should be taken to include in this commission representatives of minorities in order that the sacred rights of minorities may be effectively protected. Such a commission I believe, could solve the problems that arise and would perhaps enable us to determine the procedure we would have to follow to amend our constitution ourselves without having to apply to the British parliament.
I said, Mr. Speaker, that the second condition we must fulfil to pass through what I would call the post-war crisis is to give to domestic problems the most equitable solutions. These problems, of course, are extremely numerous, but I believe that some are more important than others. There is for instance the problem of employment about which we have heard a great deal since the opening of the session. I do not intend to labour the point, but I wish to point out that last August, on the 20th to be exact, the Trades and 'Labour Congress of Canada sent to the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) a petition the conclusions of which I shall now quote. I believe that, if accepted by the government, these conclusions would go a long way to solve the problem. Here is the concluding part of that petition dated August 20:
We realize that it is impossible to do anything without funds; that is why we are in favour of maintaining war-time taxation, in accordance with our request of April last when we asked your government to raise the exemptions to $2,400 a year for married persons and $1,000 for single persons, during this crisis. To face the crisis we are now going through we urge:
The Address-Mr. Dorion

(1)	That every worker in an essential civilian industry be granted immediately a "reconversion salary" during this period of dislocation, namely one month's salary for each year of service up to three years.
(2)	In order that the greatest number may benefit from available employment, the adoption of a maximum forty-hour week without salary reduction is recommended;
(3)	To inspire confidence and maintain the purchasing power, all general salary reductions should be banned;
(4)	Restrictions on building materials should be lifted and a housing programme launched with the same energy, ingenuity and industry which were applied to the production of urgent war material;
(5)	The immediate launching of the required public works is suggested; as well as
(6)	The speediest reconversion of all war industries which can serve in peace-time production.
To this problem of employment, the housing problem is closely allied. During recent sessions, we passed certain legislative measures intended to help Canadians build themselves new houses; but I must draw the attention of the federal authorities to the fact that these enactments, while they might easily apply in Canada's important centres and large cities, are altogether inappropriate in rural areas and in ridings similar to my own constituency of Charlevoix-Saguenay. As a matter of fact, I wrote the housing administrator not very long ago to inform him of the difficulties encountered by the people of the Charlevoix-Saguenay constituency when they applied to insurance companies for loans provided by the said enactment. Unfortunately, no solution has been found to the problem and the people of my constituency who wish to build homes in order to take advantage of this act cannot do so because the insurance companies claim that their needs are not sufficiently important and that it is not worth while to send inspectors to examine the projects and to supervise the work.
I wish to call your attention to the following letter which I received last July from the director of housing:
Sir:
Replying to your letter of July 6, I regret to inform you that we cannot do anything in regard to the reluctance shown by lending institutions to make loans in more or less remote communities.
The national housing administration cannot avail itself of any legislative authority in order to dictate to the authorized lending institutions where and when they shall make loans.
However, steps are being taken in order to enlarge as quickly as possible the field of action of lending institutions.
And this letter is signed by Mr. U. Mignon for Mr. F. W. Nicolls, director of housing.

Mr. Speaker, at this session this housing act should be amended so that it may apply as fully to rural districts as to urban centres.
Now, Mr. Speaker, there is another matter	which	should	not be	overlooked,	amatter which comes up from time to time, but	which	should	certainly	be settled	if
we are to live in peace and in harmony in this country. I refer to the grievances that are continually being aired because the rights of the French population of this country are not always fully recognized. In this respect, may. I point out that too frequently official publications of the dominion government written exclusively in English are sent to Frenchspeaking centres, both to civil servants and to French-Canadian taxpayers, who have difficulty in understanding them. Thus, for instance, I know that in regard to the selective service, the representatives of this service in the province of Quebec receive a great deal of literature written exclusively in English, and on account of their insufficient knowledge of the English language, they cannot become sufficiently acquainted with such instructions to be in a position to reply to the enquiries which they receive.
I also know that, within the last few months the government have sent in French-speaking districts of Canada, some English forms for the use of the members of the armed forces who wished to be demobilized. In this case, however, I must give credit to whom credit is due. This state of affairs in the province of Quebec having been called to my attention, I asked for French forms and I was told that they were not quite ready, which fact explained the sending of the English version, but that I would receive them as soon as possible. I am glad to state that a few days later, a fortnight, I believe, the city of Quebec and all other French parts of the province, I suppose, were supplied with the French forms.
I bring this to the attention of the authorities, because I feel that all official documents distributed through the country should be printed in French and English, so that both versions could be sent to all parts of Canada at the same time.
Another point which has been the subject of numerous conversations and newspaper articles is the matter of family allowance cheques. It seems to me that it would be the simplest thing for the federal government to have all family allowance cheques printed in both French and English, and thus fulfil a general wish. To my mind, it would be only fair to the French-Canadian population of the dominion and I hope the federal auth-

The Address- Mr. Laurendeau
orities will very soon see that those responsible have these cheques, which are distributed through the whole of Canada, printed in both official languages.
There is another point which I believe should be discussed1 and' settled very soon, if we are anxious that peace and harmony be maintained in our midst.
A while ago, I referred to the amendment of the British North America Act, issued in 1943, in connection with the redistribution of electoral seats. All hon. members will have noticed that I have put on the Order paper a resolution concerning this matter and I hope we will be given the opportunity of discussing it in the house. I hope that this year, now that the war is over, all private members, resolutions may be discussed in this house. When the house passed this amendment in 1943 it was well understood that the delay was accepted on the sole condition that this redistribution of seats would be proceeded with at the very first session following the end of the war. At this session, the government should at least appoint a committee to study the matter so as to assure satisfaction to all groups of citizens.
Mr. Speaker, in all measures passed by the Dominion government and particularly in all social legislation, of ever growing importance, consideration should be given to the rights of each and every province. Of course, it may be difficult at times to conciliate provincial autonomy with all the social measures which this parliament is called upon to adopt, but care should be taken not to deprive the provinces of their rights, because, in my opinion, they are sacred and are the foundation of the structure of our constitution. Moreover, this autonomist feeling is certainly shared by the majority of our people throughout the country, and it is quite natural. As a matter of fact, if we are asked to state our preferences, we immediately think of our birthplace, of the places where we have spent our childhood, then of our district, of the region where we live, then of the province to which we belong. Therefore, in the matter of federal legislation, enactments must necessarily take into account the autonomy of the various provinces so that their rights may at all times be entirely respected.
Mr. Speaker, we are faced at present with another very acute problem to which I believe the federal authorities should give immediate attention. I refer to the status of young men who are on the blacklists of the Department of National Defence. I am concerned with those who, for some reason or other, did not answer the call to service or who, perhaps for
some excellent reason, did not report for duty after having obtained leave from the military authorities.
Mr. Speaker, the war is over and it seems to me the federal government should show leniency and generosity. It should see to it that these young men are not treated as criminals and hunted down as they are at the present time. As an example I need only to relate what happened last week in my county, in the parish of Chateau-Richer. During the night of September 12 the military police raided the parish and forced their way into private homes. Let me mention a pitiful case. The military police forced their way into the home of a sick woman to search the premises, with the result that this woman is now seriously ill in the hospital.
Mr. Speaker, such a situation should be ended. These young men who are not criminals, but who may have broken the laws of the country in wartime, should no longer be pursued. To-day, now that the war is over, we should consider giving them the benefit of an amnesty. Besides, the Liberal members should have no trouble in understanding my request, as I could refer them to the speeches they made in 1919. At that time, after the last war, when the government kept on hunting down the recruits, as we se it done to-day, the members of the opposition of the time clamoured for, and rightly so, the amnesty of the so-called deserters.
These questions may come up again for discussion during this session, but I thought I would bring them to-day to the attention of the house and particularly of the government.

Mr. Speaker, it is customary for the hon. members of this house, at the beginning of a new parliament, to congratulate the Speaker on his election. I do so with much pleasure because he is a personal friend of mine who has had something to do with my entrance into public life, and who has studied in the same college and the same university. I am pleased to see him again to-day in the post which he now occupies in this house. I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that you will preside over the debates of this house with tactfulness and judgment and that, true to Liberal traditions, you will give your rulings with justice and to the satisfaction of all members of this house.
I also wish to congratulate the mover and the seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne.
